title: Pastoral Health: A Study for Leaders and Those Who Love Them
subtitle: A plainspoken five-session study on the exhaustion, hiddenness, and quiet despair of the people who shepherd us, for boards and leadership teams to read alongside the pastor they're trying to keep.
summary:
This study is for elder boards, deacon teams, leadership councils, and the spouses and friends who love a pastor and can see he's tired in a way that worries them. Its five sessions ask why faithful pastors leave, why so many are quietly depressed, how a man can lose his soul while building a church, why his hidden life is the first thing to starve, and why a church should require its pastor to rest. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note for the leader, every session has a case to talk through, and every session ends in prayer rather than a plan.

It won't scold the pastor for being weak or the board for being blind. It asks something harder: that the leadership look at a way of doing church they helped build, one that can wear out the most faithful man in the room and then mourn him in real confusion about what went wrong. Read it with your own pastor in the room, or at least with his face in your mind.

A plain word before you begin. This material touches burnout, and in two sessions it touches clinical depression directly. Depression is not a failure of faith, and exhaustion is not a character flaw. Where a pastor is struggling with depression or any mental illness, the right and faithful step is a medical doctor and a licensed counselor, the same as for any other illness of the body. If a pastor is in crisis, call or text 988. Seeking help is an act of faith, not a confession of failure. There is no shame anywhere in this room.
audience: Pastors, elder boards, and church leadership teams

sessions.title: Why Pastors Are Leaving
sessions.aim: To see that the pastors who leave are often the most faithful, worn out by a kind of work we built that was never the work they were called to, so a board can stop calling the loss turnover and start naming the wound.
sessions.summary:
Many pastors reach the point of saying they're done. Not in scandal, not in doubt about God, just done, after years with a congregation that loved them and emptied them in roughly equal measure. Often they can't name what broke, and that should frighten us. Conflict, money, and the elders are usually where an older wound finally tears open, not the wound itself.

In 2021 Barna found that 38 percent of Protestant pastors had seriously considered quitting full-time ministry in the previous year. Some say the exodus is a correction, shaking out men who were never suited for the work, and there's truth in that. But the men bleeding out are often the devoted ones, who gave the work everything they had.

Elijah is the map. After fire fell on Carmel, he ran into the wilderness and asked God to take his life. God didn't rebuke him. He gave him bread, sleep, a question, and in time a companion, because part of what broke Elijah was the belief that he stood alone. We aren't losing pastors because the work is hard. We're losing them because we've built a work that asks a man to spend himself for a master who isn't Christ.

keyScripture.why: "He asked that he might die, saying, 'It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers'" (1 Kings 19:4). Elijah prays this just after the greatest victory of his ministry. Collapse can follow triumph, and it isn't the same as failure.

discussion.q: Many pastors who leave can't name what broke them. Why is a wound a faithful man can't name more dangerous than one he can?
discussion.behind: Help the board see that the real injury is rarely the presenting issue. Conflict and budget are where an older exhaustion finally tears open. If a man can't name it, neither can his elders, so they'll treat the symptom and miss the wound. Land it on paying attention, not on alarm.

discussion.q: Some say the pastors leaving were never built for it, and the church is simply being sorted. What's true in that? And which pastors does it fail to explain?
discussion.behind: Not every man ordained should have been, and an honest exit beats a faithless tenure. But the devoted are often the ones who burn, because they gave the work everything. If a board assumes the strong stay and the weak leave, it may have things backward. Ask people to picture a specific faithful pastor they've known, not a category.

discussion.q: Read 1 Kings 19:1-18. God doesn't give Elijah a strategy. He gives him bread, sleep, a question, and a companion. What does that say to a board that wants to fix a tired pastor with a new plan?
discussion.behind: Boards reach for programs because programs are what boards know how to give. The passage doesn't. The first care for an emptied man is food, rest, a real question, and the end of his isolation. Listen for the board member who realizes his first instinct was to schedule something.

discussion.q: Twice Elijah says, "I, even I only, am left" (1 Kings 19:10, 14), and it isn't true. Where might your pastor be carrying a story of being alone that people in this room could quietly disprove?
discussion.behind: Isolation is often a story more than a fact, and the story can be deadly. Move the board from sympathy to a concrete sense of how a pastor gets cut off and what their own presence could undo. Don't let it stay abstract. Ask who in the room actually knows him.

discussion.q: Many pastors pour themselves out without limit because nobody taught them they could be loved without earning it. Where do you see that earning in your pastor, or in yourself?
discussion.behind: Go gently, and go first if you're leading. This isn't a hunt for the pastor's flaws. It's noticing that a whole way of life can run on earned love. The board member who has built his own worth on what he produces will recognize it, because he's in it too.

objections.objection: Most pastors who leave just weren't cut out for the work. This is making excuses for men who couldn't handle the pressure everyone in ministry signs up for.
objections.response: Half of that is true. Not every man ordained should have been, and an honest exit is better than a faithless tenure. But the men the church is losing aren't mostly the casual ones. They're the ones who prayed, visited the dying, and preached at real cost. The "they weren't cut out for it" theory explains people at the edges and fails at the center, where the most faithful are bleeding out. Pressure isn't the problem. A kind of work that requires a man to spend himself for the wrong master is.

objections.objection: Ministry is supposed to cost. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. All this talk of burnout sounds like excusing pastors from the sacrifice the calling has always demanded.
objections.response: That conviction is biblical, and this study doesn't back away from it. Sacrifice is the calling. The question is what a pastor is being spent on and whether anything refills him. A man can be poured out for Christ and rest in him, or poured out for a congregation's approval and be consumed by a god that blesses nothing. The first is sacrifice. The second is a slow death we've learned to call dedication, and a board's job is to know the difference.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When did you last ask your pastor how he is and actually wait, in silence, for the true answer instead of the one he gives in the hallway?
sessions.practice: This week, one member of this board reaches out to the pastor with no agenda, no problem to solve, and no meeting attached. Just bread: a meal, a walk, a note that asks for nothing. Notice whether that's harder for you than scheduling a task, and ask yourself why.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you fed your prophet under the broom tree when he asked you to take his life, and you didn't rebuke him. You gave him bread and sleep and a friend. Teach us to love our pastor the way you loved Elijah, without a strategy or a fix, just with presence. Show us where he's carrying the belief that he stands alone, and let us be the people who quietly prove it false. Guard the faithful among us, and keep us from losing them and calling it turnover. In the name of the Good Shepherd, amen.
reflection: Have we as a board treated our pastor's exhaustion as a problem to manage rather than a person to feed? What would change if we stopped?
Where in my own life have I earned love until I was hollow, and how does that help me see what my pastor may be doing?
If our pastor were running on fumes right now, would we know? Who in this room is close enough to him to tell?
sessions.teaching:
For a lot of boards this begins with a phone call, and by then it's late. A pastor calls a friend and says he's done. Not because of a scandal, not because he stopped believing in God, just done, the way a man says it after he's already cleaned out his office. He gave years to a congregation that loved him and emptied him in roughly equal measure. And here's the part that should frighten a board: he can't name what broke.

Pause there before reaching for an explanation, because the reaching is part of the problem. We say a man left over conflict, money, the elders, or trouble at home, and sometimes those things are real. But they're rarely the wound. They're the place where an older exhaustion finally tears open. If the most faithful man in your church can't name what broke him, you probably can't either, and you'll treat the tear and miss the wound. The numbers are real. In 2021 Barna found that 38 percent of Protestant pastors had seriously considered quitting full-time ministry within the previous year. Something sped up, and the question is whether a board understands what.

The case against alarm deserves its full weight. Some say the exodus is a correction: the men leaving were never built for it, and the culture is shaking out the casual. There's truth in it. Not every man ordained should have been. Eugene Peterson warned that in many men the vocation of pastor has been replaced by the profession of running a religious business, and a man can be good at the business without ever having been a pastor. If those men leave, that's honesty, not loss. But the theory fails at the center. The men actually bleeding out aren't the casual ones. They're the ones who prayed, who sat with the dying, who preached texts that cost them. The theory works at the edges and can't explain the man who couldn't name what broke him, because he was the most devoted person in the room.

So I keep going back to the broom tree. Elijah has just seen fire fall on Mount Carmel, the greatest victory of his ministry. Then he runs into the wilderness, sits down under a tree, and asks God to let him die: "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life" (1 Kings 19:4). This isn't a man who failed. He won, and the winning emptied him, and in the emptiness the only prayer he could find was a prayer to die.

Watch what God doesn't do. He doesn't hand Elijah a strategy or a recovery plan. He gives him bread and water and lets him sleep. Then the angel wakes him to eat again, because, the text says, the road ahead is too much for him (1 Kings 19:7). Then, at the mountain, he asks him a question: "What are you doing here, Elijah?" (1 Kings 19:9). And in the end he gives him a companion in Elisha, because part of what broke Elijah was the belief that he was alone. "I, even I only, am left," he says twice (1 Kings 19:10, 14), and both times it isn't true. God tells him there are seven thousand in Israel who haven't bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:18). The isolation was a story he told himself, and it nearly killed him.

A board that wants to fix a tired pastor with a new program is reaching for the very thing this passage refuses. The first care for an emptied man is bread, rest, a real question, and the end of his aloneness. Plenty of pastors know this from the inside. Nobody taught them a man could be loved without earning it, so they earned until they were hollow. A church can run on that kind of earned love without anyone meaning it to, and the devoted are the ones it uses up.

We aren't losing pastors because the work is hard. We're losing them because we've built a version of the work that asks a man to spend himself for a master who isn't Christ: approval, attendance, being needed. Name that master. Then do what God did for Elijah, and bring the bread.

scriptureStudy.note: Elijah "was afraid, and he arose and ran for his life," and he left his servant behind. The collapse begins with isolation. He strips away his last companion before the despair sets in.
He walks a day into the wilderness "and came and sat down under a broom tree." Notice where burnout takes him: away from people, alone, in a barren place. His body acts out the state of his soul.
"It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life." This comes not after defeat but after the greatest victory of his ministry. Triumph emptied him.

"He lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, 'Arise and eat.'" God's first answer to the death wish is a meal and sleep, not a rebuke. The body is fed first.

The angel comes "a second time" with "Arise and eat," and tells him why: the road ahead is too great for him. God says the load is too heavy. He doesn't say the man is too weak. His diagnosis honors the prophet instead of shaming him.
"I, even I only, am left." The belief at the center of Elijah's despair is that he's alone, and he says it twice as if repeating it made it true.

"Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal." God answers the isolation with a fact. The cure isn't a pep talk. It's the truth that he was never as alone as exhaustion told him.

sessions.goingDeeper:
A group that wants to go further can look at how the role itself has been framed, because part of the wound is built into it. Peterson's distinction between the vocation of a pastor and the profession of running a religious business has a history behind it. Across the late twentieth century the senior pastor increasingly became a chief executive. Management thinking that served companies well was applied to congregations, and the church-growth movement taught a generation to measure faithfulness by attendance and budget. Something was gained in reach and organization. Something was lost when we trained men to grow enterprises and called it shepherding.

Henri Nouwen is a good companion here. He left a teaching post at Harvard for L'Arche, a community of people with intellectual disabilities, and in In the Name of Jesus he described the minister's temptations as the pull to be relevant, spectacular, and powerful. The way back, he argued, runs downward, toward weakness and being known by God rather than by the crowd.

For a board the hard question isn't how to keep pastors. It's whether the role you've handed your pastor is the one Christ called him to, or a corporate office with a pulpit in it. A structure can be efficient, growing, and admired and still be exactly what wears out the most faithful man inside it. Attrition numbers measure the symptom. Only an honest look at the role tells a board what it actually built.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose your pastor has been with you nine years. Attendance is steady, the budget is met, nobody's complaining. But the board chair notices he's stopped answering texts the same day, his sermons lean more on old notes, and he canceled the last two elder lunches with a vague excuse. At the meeting someone says he may be coasting and suggests a frank talk about his work ethic, maybe a review of his hours. Heads nod, because a review is something boards know how to do.

That instinct treats a tired man as a lazy one. What if the slower replies and the old notes aren't a discipline problem at all, but a man under the broom tree, running on fumes and too ashamed to say so to the people who evaluate him?

The faithful move isn't a performance review. It's bread. One person reaches out with no agenda: a meal, a walk, a real question, and the patience to wait for the true answer. Understand the wound before you manage the symptom, and don't let the room turn exhaustion into a charge.

devotional.title: The Thing He Couldn't Name
devotional.body:
A pastor who has given years to a church that loves him can call and say he's done, and not be able to say what broke. We're quick to supply a name for him: the conflict, the budget, the hard family in the third row. Sometimes those are real, but they're rarely the wound. They're where an older exhaustion finally tore open. Elijah sat under the broom tree after his greatest victory and couldn't name it either. He only knew it was enough.

If you love a pastor, resist the urge to explain his tiredness for him so the discomfort of not knowing can be put away. An unnamed wound can't be treated until it's found, and finding it takes patience. Today, instead of explaining him, pray for eyes to see him. Ask God to show you the older wound under the presenting problem, and ask whether your quickness to name it has kept you from staying long enough to find it.
devotional.prayer: Father, I'm quick to explain what I should slow down to see. Give me patience to sit with what I can't yet name in the people I love. Show me the wound under the wound, and keep me from treating a tear and missing the injury.

devotional.title: Bread Before Strategy
devotional.body:
When Elijah asked to die, God didn't give him a plan. He gave him bread. An angel touched him and said, "Arise and eat," and there was a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. He ate, slept, and was woken to eat again before a single word of correction.

Read that against every instinct to fix a tired person with a program. The first care for an emptied servant is the care of the body, because a body that hasn't slept will lie to a man about God and about whether morning is worth getting up for. We schedule and strategize and hand the exhausted a new system. God baked bread.

If there's a worn-out person in your life, a pastor or anyone else, ask today whether you've been offering strategy when what they need is a meal and permission to sleep. The most spiritual thing you can do for someone under their own broom tree may sound the least spiritual: feed them, let them rest, and ask nothing yet.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you fed your prophet before you questioned him, and I reach for strategy when you reach for bread. Teach me to care for the bodies of the weary, to offer rest before a plan, and to ask nothing until they're fed.

devotional.title: I Only Am Left
devotional.body:
Twice Elijah says it: "I, even I only, am left." Both times it isn't true. Seven thousand in Israel had not bowed to Baal. The isolation that nearly killed him was a story, but it didn't feel like a story. It felt like the plain truth of a man who had given everything and, as far as he could see, stood alone.

That's how isolation often works in the people who serve us. It's less a fact than a story, and the people who could disprove it rarely get close enough to try. Think today of someone you suspect is carrying that story: a pastor, a leader, a friend who holds everyone and feels held by no one. You may be one of the seven thousand who could quietly prove it false. Not with a speech about how he isn't really alone, but by drawing near and refusing to let him be.
devotional.prayer: Father, you answered Elijah's loneliness with a fact and a friend. Show me who near me believes they stand alone, and make me the proof that they don't. Let me draw near to the ones who hold everyone and feel held by no one.

devotional.title: The Earning That Hollows
devotional.body:
Many pastors pour themselves out without limit because nobody taught them a man could be loved without earning it, so they earn until they're hollow. That isn't only a pastor's problem. It runs most of us: the quiet belief that love is a wage, and we'd better keep working or it'll stop.

The son in Jesus' parable came home rehearsing a speech about becoming a hired servant. He wanted to negotiate his way back onto the payroll. But "while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him." The father wouldn't let love be a wage.

Find the place today where you're earning, where your sense of being loved by God or valued by people rests on your usefulness. It will hollow you the way it hollows many pastors, and it hides easily inside good work. Ask God to let you receive a love you can't earn or lose, and to show you how the same fear may be emptying a leader you love.
devotional.prayer: Father who ran toward the son who'd earned nothing, I've believed love was a wage and worked myself hollow to keep it. Teach me to receive what I can't earn. Free me, and the people I love, from the fear that rest will cost us your love.

devotional.title: A Master Who Isn't Christ
devotional.body:
The hardest sentence in this session is that we aren't losing pastors because the work is hard, but because we've built a work that asks a man to spend himself for a master who isn't Christ. A congregation's approval can become a god, and that god demands everything and blesses nothing. A man can break the first commandment in the holiest-sounding way there is, by making the church his master instead of the church's Lord.

Jesus offers a different yoke: "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." He doesn't offer no yoke. He offers his own, under a gentle master who gives rest.

Ask today whose yoke your pastor is under, and whose you're under. Is it the gentle Lord, or a master made of approval and attendance and being needed? Name it truthfully, and then come to the only yoke that doesn't break the one who wears it.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, gentle and lowly, I've worn yokes you never gave me and called them faithfulness. Show me the master that isn't you. Free my pastor, and free me, to take the only yoke that gives rest instead of taking the soul. Amen.

sessions.title: Depression in the Pulpit
sessions.aim: To name a pastor's depression plainly as an illness that can sit inside deep faith, to strip away the shame the church has built around it, and to point clearly to a doctor and a counselor as faithful first steps.
sessions.summary:
Many pastors have preached on the goodness of God on a morning they couldn't feel it, their chests full of lead, telling a room about a joy they couldn't find in themselves. There's a sentence pastors learn to say without believing it: "I'm fine."

The strongest objection is theological: depression in a shepherd is finally a failure of faith. It can't survive the Bible. The Psalms are full of faithful people in despair. Jeremiah curses the day he was born. Job longs for death. Elijah asks to die. If despair were always faithlessness, the most faithful people in Scripture were the most faithless. God doesn't rebuke Elijah. He sends an angel who says, twice, "Arise and eat." The first care for the despairing prophet is food and sleep.

In 2014 a Lifeway Research study found that nearly a quarter of pastors had personally struggled with some kind of mental illness. Depression is often an illness of body and brain, and the faithful response is a doctor and a licensed counselor. And a man who has been to the floor and found God still there can preach with a weight nobody can fake. At the cross Jesus cried, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" There's no floor of despair where Christ hasn't already been.

keyScripture.why: "And the angel of the LORD came again a second time and touched him and said, 'Arise and eat'" (1 Kings 19:7), because the road ahead was too much for him. God's first care for a crushed servant is the care of the body, food and sleep, not a sterner sermon.

discussion.q: Pastors learn to say "I'm fine" until it runs without the soul behind it. Why would a church make it so costly for a pastor to tell the truth about how he is?
discussion.behind: Help the board see it may be part of what punishes the truth. Elders who'd panic at a hard answer teach the pastor to give a smooth one. Ask what the room's own reaction to bad news has trained him to hide. Land it on safety, not blame.

discussion.q: Some say a truly faithful man wouldn't be crushed. Read Psalm 42:5, Jeremiah 20:14-18, and 1 Kings 19:4. Why does it matter that some of Scripture's most faithful people were also its most despairing?
discussion.behind: This is what removes the shame. If despair were always faithlessness, the saints were the worst sinners, which is absurd. You want the board to stop reading a depressed pastor as a spiritual failure and start seeing a person to be fed. Tie it to how God actually treats Elijah.

discussion.q: God's first care for Elijah is bread and sleep, not more Scripture memory and a sterner devotional life. What does that teach a board about the difference between a spiritual problem and a medical one?
discussion.behind: Be plain here. Depression is often an illness of body and brain, and the faithful response is a doctor and a licensed counselor, as for any other illness. A board that only prescribes more prayer for a depressed pastor may be withholding the bread God himself sent. Say clearly that if a pastor is in crisis, call or text 988.

discussion.q: A 2014 Lifeway Research study found that nearly a quarter of pastors had personally struggled with some kind of mental illness. Why might pastors tell even an anonymous survey that they're fine?
discussion.behind: The habit of performing wellness runs so deep it can survive anonymity. For a board the arithmetic is sobering: among the pastors you know, several are likely struggling and saying nothing. Move the room toward making it normal, even expected, for a pastor to see a counselor, so that getting help looks like health rather than collapse.

discussion.q: Many pastors tell no one for far too long because they're supposed to be the ones who carry others. Where might that kind of pride be keeping your pastor silent? What would this room actually do if he said he wasn't okay?
discussion.behind: Be tender. A pastor's silence can be pride dressed as humility, a refusal to let the body of Christ see that he bleeds. A board can't order a man out of that, but it can lower the cost of the truth. Make the second question concrete.

objections.objection: Calling a pastor's despair a medical condition just excuses a spiritual failure. Therapy culture renames every sin a wound and lets everyone off the hook.
objections.response: There is a therapy culture that dissolves all sin into syndrome, and it's wrong. But this objection fails on its own ground. The Bible it means to honor is full of faithful people in despair whom God feeds instead of rebuking. Calling depression an illness doesn't excuse sin. It refuses to call an illness a sin. The faithful response is a doctor and a counselor, as for any sickness of the body, and treating it that way is obedience, not evasion.

objections.objection: If our pastor is depressed, that's a private matter between him and God. It's not the board's business to go poking into his mental health.
objections.response: The instinct toward privacy is right in part. A pastor's inner life doesn't belong to the board. But the point isn't surveillance. It's care: making it safe for him to speak and making sure he has real help when he does. A board doesn't diagnose. It removes the shame, covers the cost of counseling, protects his time to get well, and in a crisis acts without hesitation. If a pastor is ever in danger, call or text 988, and do not treat his life as too private to protect. Love here isn't intrusion. It's the bread God sent the angel to bake.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you woke one morning unable to find a single reason to care, who would you tell? Does your pastor have anyone like that?
sessions.practice: This week, find out, quietly and without alarm, whether your church covers counseling for the pastor and his family, and whether he has a physician and a counselor he actually sees. If the answer is no, start the work of making it yes. Frame it everywhere as health, never as a problem.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you went into the dark and cried out that you were forsaken, so there's no floor of despair where you haven't already been. Thank you that a man in the pulpit who feels forsaken is standing where the gospel happened. Take the shame off our pastor. Give him a brother, a physician, a counselor, and a friend who will bring bread instead of a sermon. Make this church a place where weakness can be spoken and met. And where any of your servants is in danger, move us to act quickly and without fear. Amen.
reflection: What would I actually do if my pastor told me he was depressed? Would that reaction make it safer or harder for him to tell me?
Have I ever treated mental illness as a spiritual failure rather than an illness? Where did I learn that?
Does our church make seeing a counselor look like faith or like collapse? What would it take to change the answer?
sessions.teaching:
I can't write about this from a safe distance. Pastors have stood in pulpits with their chests full of lead and told a room about the goodness of God, a joy they couldn't, in that hour, find in themselves. Some of the people who shepherd you have done exactly that, and the not talking about it is part of the sickness.

There's a sentence pastors learn to say without believing it: "I'm fine." They say it in the hallway with a smile perfected over years. They say it to elders who would panic at any other answer. They say it to their wives until their wives stop believing it and start grieving in silence beside them. A smile like that is a skill, and a skill can be practiced until it runs without the soul behind it.

The strongest objection deserves to be heard, because sincere people make it. Depression in a believer, and especially in a shepherd, is finally a failure of faith, they'd say. "The joy of the LORD is your strength" (Nehemiah 8:10). If a man truly believed the gospel he preaches, he wouldn't be crushed, and calling his despair a medical condition only excuses a spiritual one. And there is a therapy culture that dissolves every sin into a syndrome. I won't defend it.

But the objection can't survive the Bible it means to honor. The Psalms are full of faithful people in deep despair: "Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me?" (Psalm 42:5). Jeremiah curses the day he was born. Job, whom God calls blameless, longs for death. Elijah, fresh from calling down fire, asks God to take his life. If despair were always faithlessness, the most faithful people in Scripture were the most faithless, and that's absurd.

Look at how God treats Elijah. He doesn't rebuke the collapse. He treats it as a body and soul to be fed. An angel touches him and says, "Arise and eat" (1 Kings 19:5), and then comes a second time with the same words, because the road ahead is too much for him (1 Kings 19:7). The first care for the despairing prophet is food and sleep. The body is where the soul lives, and a body that hasn't slept in weeks will lie to a man about God and about whether morning is worth getting up for.

That's the model, and a board needs to be plain about it. Depression is often an illness of the body and the brain, and the faithful response is a doctor and a licensed counselor, as it would be for any other illness. A board that prescribes only more prayer and a sterner devotional life for a depressed pastor may be withholding the very bread God sent the angel to bake. Say it clearly in the room. Getting help is faith, not failure. There's no shame here. And if a pastor is ever in crisis, call or text 988.

In 2014 a Lifeway Research study found that nearly a quarter of pastors had personally struggled with some kind of mental illness. I suspect the real number is higher, since pastors have a well-practiced habit of telling surveys they're fine. Think about the pastors you know, and feel the weight of that.

And there's something the smiling version of faith can't hold. A pastor's despair isn't always his disqualification. A man who has been to the floor and found God still there preaches resurrection with a weight nobody can fake. Henri Nouwen called this the wounded healer: the minister whose own wounds, offered rather than hidden, become a source of healing for others. Beneath every floor is the cross. On it Jesus cried out, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). God himself entered the dark, so there's no basement of human despair where Christ hasn't already been. The man in the pulpit who feels forsaken is standing exactly where the gospel happened.

So tell someone. A brother, a physician, a counselor, a friend who will bring bread instead of a sermon. The God who fed Elijah isn't ashamed of your weakness. Shame is the only voice saying otherwise, and shame lies.

scriptureStudy.note: Elijah asks to die after his greatest victory. Despair sits here inside deep faith, not against it. That's why the church can stop reading a crushed servant as a spiritual failure.

"And he lay down and slept." The first thing the text records after the death wish is sleep. Exhaustion of the body is named before anything spiritual, because the body isn't a distraction from the soul. It's where the soul lives.

"An angel touched him and said to him, 'Arise and eat.'" The care is physical and gentle, a touch and a meal. God meets the despairing prophet first as a body that needs food, the way a doctor meets an illness.
"He ate and drank and lay down again." One round of care isn't enough. God lets him sleep again before asking anything, a patience with recovery that doesn't rush the broken back to work.

The LORD isn't in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire, but in "the sound of a low whisper." The God who answered Baal's prophets with fire answers his broken servant quietly. He doesn't shout at a man already on the floor.

"Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God." The psalmist speaks to his own soul from inside the despair. Faith here isn't the absence of the dark. It's talking truth to yourself in it.
"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" At the cross God himself entered the dark and the cry of forsakenness. There's no floor of despair where Christ hasn't gone ahead of the sufferer.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Hold the clinical and the theological together without folding one into the other, because that's where a board can do real harm or real good. Depression often has biological roots and responds to medical care, and treating it that way isn't a concession to a secular age. It's following the God who fed Elijah's body before he spoke to his soul. A doctor and a licensed counselor are faithful first steps, the same as for any illness of the body, and if a pastor is in crisis the board acts at once and calls or texts 988.

Some of the shame has a history. Folk theology has long read suffering as either punishment or weak faith, and parts of twentieth-century American church culture added the ideal of the always-victorious Christian and the always-smiling pastor. It wasn't always so. Charles Spurgeon, the most famous preacher in Victorian London, lived with depression for much of his life, and in his Lectures to My Students (1875) he wrote plainly, "Fits of depression come over the most of us." His generation had room for the suffering saint in a way ours often hasn't.

The work for a board is to recover what we lost. Make a counselor look as ordinary as a physical therapist. Cover the cost. Normalize it before there's a crisis. And know the line you don't cross: a board doesn't diagnose, doesn't pry, and doesn't treat a man's inner life as its property. It removes the shame, funds the help, protects the time to get well, and in danger acts without hesitation. Nouwen's wounded healer is the hope underneath it all. A board isn't managing a liability. It's caring for a man whose wounds, met by God, may one day help heal others.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose that late on a Tuesday your pastor sits across from two elders and says quietly that he hasn't felt like himself in months, that some mornings he can't find a reason to get up, and that he's scared. The room goes still. One elder's first instinct is encouragement: remind him of all the good he does and all the people who love him, pray, and send him home lighter.

That instinct is kind, and it isn't enough. What he's described isn't discouragement to be talked out of. It may be an illness that needs a doctor. Receive what he said as the brave and faithful act it is. Say plainly that this isn't a failure of faith. Help him that week to a physician and a licensed counselor, with the church covering the cost.

And hear the weight of what he said about mornings. If there's any sign he's in danger, don't treat it as too private to touch. You stay with him, and you call or text 988. Don't let the room comfort him back into silence. Make it safe for him to have said the hardest sentence he's ever said, and then make sure he isn't carrying it alone.

memoryVerse.text: And the angel of the LORD came again a second time and touched him and said, "Arise and eat."

devotional.title: The Sermon He Couldn't Feel
devotional.body:
Pastors have preached on the goodness of God on mornings they couldn't feel it, telling a room about a joy they couldn't find in themselves. If you've never carried that, today is a day to learn compassion for those who have, and some of them stand in pulpits.

The psalmist asks, "Why are you cast down, O my soul?" and answers, "Hope in God." He doesn't pretend the dark isn't there. He speaks truth to his soul from inside it. That isn't hypocrisy, and it isn't failed faith. It's one of the oldest experiences of the faithful.

Today, lay down any picture of the Christian life with no room for the cast-down soul. Ask for a faith truthful enough to say "I am cast down" and still turn toward God, and for the tenderness to let the people you love tell you about their darkness without fearing your judgment.
devotional.prayer: Father, some of the most faithful in your Scripture were the most cast down, and you didn't turn from them. Give me a faith that can name the dark, and a heart safe enough that the people I love can name theirs to me.

devotional.title: Arise and Eat
devotional.body:
God's first care for the prophet who wanted to die wasn't a sermon. It was a meal and a nap. An angel touched him, let him sleep, woke him to eat again, and only later did God speak. A body that hasn't slept will lie to a man about God and hope and whether morning is worth rising for.

This opens a door the church has sometimes kept shut. Sometimes despair is an illness of the body and the brain, and the faithful response is the care of a doctor and a counselor, as for any other sickness. There's no shame in it, and seeking that help is an act of faith. If you or someone you love is in crisis, call or text 988, and treat it as the urgent thing it is.

Hold this today against any voice that says a true believer can pray his way out of every darkness. God baked bread for Elijah. He didn't shame him. Pointing someone toward a doctor isn't less spiritual. It's faithful.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you fed your prophet's body before you spoke to his soul, and you weren't ashamed of his weakness. Make me unashamed too. Teach me to offer real help, to call an illness an illness, and to act quickly in a crisis.

devotional.title: The Low Whisper
devotional.body:
After the bread and the sleep, God brought Elijah to the mountain. He wasn't in the wind, or the earthquake, or the fire. After the fire came "the sound of a low whisper." The God who answered Baal's prophets with fire answered his broken servant with quiet. He doesn't shout at a man already on the floor.

We could learn to treat each other that way, and ourselves. When someone is at the bottom, the loud cure is usually wrong: the stern lecture, the stack of verses, the demand to snap out of it. Ask today whether you've brought wind and fire to people who needed quiet. And if you're the one on the floor, hear that the God who meets the broken doesn't come to scold. He comes close and gently, and the gentleness is the shape of his care.
devotional.prayer: Father, you came to your broken prophet in a whisper, not in fire. Forgive the times I've brought noise to people who needed quiet. Teach me your gentleness with the suffering, and let me hear it for myself when I'm the one on the floor.

devotional.title: Pride Dressed as Humility
devotional.body:
Pastors often tell no one for far too long, because they're supposed to be the ones who carry. Hiding despair to protect a reputation isn't humility. It's pride dressed as humility, a refusal to let the body of Christ see that you bleed.

James says, "Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed." The healing runs through being known. The instinct to carry it alone feels like strength, but it's a wall, and behind it a person can drown in private.

Look at your own silence today. Where are you hiding a struggle or a fear because being seen feels more dangerous than suffering alone? Ask for the harder courage: to tell one safe person who will bring bread and not a sermon. And ask how you might be that safe person for someone else.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I've called my hiding humility when it was pride. Give me courage to tell one safe person the truth. And make me that safe person for someone else, who meets weakness with bread and not a sermon.

devotional.title: Where the Gospel Happened
devotional.body:
On the cross Jesus cried, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" The Savior went into the experience of being forsaken, so that forsakenness would never be the last word over his people. There's no basement of human despair where Christ hasn't already been. A man in the pulpit who feels forsaken isn't outside the gospel. He's standing where it happened.

This isn't a verse to use on someone's pain to make it stop. It's company offered from inside the pain. If you're in the dark today, Christ isn't far off and disappointed. He's near, and he knows this cry. If someone you love is in the dark, don't preach this at them from above. Stay in it with them, because that is what Christ does, and point them, gently and practically, to the help that faith provides, a doctor, a counselor, and in a crisis the number 988.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, you cried out that you were forsaken so that I never would be. Meet me and the people I love on whatever floor we're lying on. Let me never be ashamed of the help you provide, and let me sit with the suffering the way you sit with me. Amen.

sessions.title: Leading Without Losing the Soul
sessions.aim: To see that a pastor can build a thriving church and lose the soul that was meant to lead it, and that the cure isn't less sacrifice but a source the sacrifice can't empty.
sessions.summary:
Jesus asked, "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?" (Mark 8:36), and he asked it of disciples who wanted to be great. A pastor can lose his soul building a kingdom and call the loss sacrifice. From the outside it looks like success.

Some will say ministry is meant to cost, and a pastor forever guarding his peace will never go to the hospital at two in the morning. That's true. Sacrifice is the calling. But a pastor has to be filled from a source the spending can't empty. He isn't a candle that gives light by burning down to nothing. He's a branch that bears fruit because it's fed. "Apart from me you can do nothing," Jesus says (John 15:5). Not less. Nothing.

From the 1970s on, the American church took on the language of corporate management, and the pastor became a chief executive. Eugene Peterson called much of what followed a betrayal of the pastor's real work. The family therapist Edwin Friedman argued that what matters most in a leader is a calm, steady presence, not technique. And the cross says the decisive work is already finished, which is why a pastor can work hard and then sleep.

keyScripture.why: "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing" (John 15:5). A branch cut off from the vine produces nothing, however busy it looks.

discussion.q: A soul going dry can look like success from the outside: attendance up, staff growing, the well running dry. How would a board even see that, when every visible sign is good?
discussion.behind: The danger is that the numbers a board watches are the ones that hide the wound. Attendance can climb while a man preaches from memory of a God he used to know. Ask what the board actually measures, and whether any of it would catch a soul going dry.

discussion.q: A candle gives light by burning itself up. A branch bears fruit because it's fed. Which has your church been quietly asking your pastor to be?
discussion.behind: A board can admire a candle right down to the stub and call it dedication. The point isn't that the pastor should give less but that he has to be fed, and the board has a part in whether he is. Listen for the person who realizes they've been admiring the burning.

discussion.q: Read John 15:1-8. "Apart from me you can do nothing." What does it mean that a busy, fruitful-looking ministry could amount to a large, visible nothing?
discussion.behind: This should unsettle the room. A cut branch can look impressive while it withers. Protecting the pastor's life with God isn't a soft extra. It's the condition of anything real getting built. Tie it to the difference between activity and fruit.

discussion.q: Edwin Friedman argued that what matters most in a leader is the ability to stay calm and connected without being driven by everyone else's anxiety. How does a worn-out pastor end up absorbing every fear in the church?
discussion.behind: A pastor with no inner ground picks up every anxiety around him and can't lead because he has nowhere to lead from. That makes his hidden life practical, not optional. His prayer isn't time away from leading. It's where leading comes from. Ask how the church's own anxiety lands on him.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 127:1-2. If a man can't rest, what is that saying about who he thinks is building the house? Where do you see that in your pastor, or in yourself?
discussion.behind: Go first. Most board members run their own lives on the same quiet unbelief. The goal isn't guilt but freedom: the gospel lets a man work hard and then sleep, because the saving work is finished.

objections.objection: All this concern for the pastor's soul is a comfortable gospel dressed up as wisdom. Ministry is meant to cost, and a pastor forever guarding his peace will never go to the hospital at two in the morning.
objections.response: That's right as far as it goes. Sacrifice is the calling, and a pastor who only protects himself has abandoned the sheep. But the argument isn't that he should spend himself less. It's that he has to be filled from a source the spending can't empty. A branch fed by the vine can pour itself out at a hospital bed at two in the morning and then sleep without guilt, because the sleep is trust that the vine keeps feeding the branch while it rests. The cure for a candle isn't less burning. It's becoming a branch.

objections.objection: If the pastor needs all this solitude and rest to function, maybe he just isn't strong enough for the job. A real leader pushes through.
objections.response: Look at the picture of strength behind that. The pastor who never stops, pushing through on stored-up reserves, may be the cut branch producing a busy nothing. Pushing through is exactly how a man loses his soul building a kingdom and calls it sacrifice. The calm, steady presence Friedman described isn't weakness. It's one of the deepest strengths a leader has, and it grows in the hidden life this objection wants to cut. A board that prizes the man who never stops is prizing the thing that will eventually break him.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you picture your pastor on an ordinary Thursday with nothing required of him, do you imagine him at rest in God, or already hurrying to the next task?
sessions.practice: This week, look at one thing your board asks of the pastor that mainly keeps the organization moving, and ask whether it feeds the branch or strips it. Bring one thing you could take off his plate, not add to it, to the next meeting.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you are the vine and our pastor is a branch, and apart from you he can do nothing, however busy the doing looks. Forgive us for asking him to be a candle, burning down to nothing, and calling it dedication. Keep him joined to you. Let the fruit of this church grow from a man who is fed, not one who is drying up at the stem. And teach all of us that you build the house, so that we and he can finally sleep. Amen.
reflection: What do we as a board actually measure? Would any of it tell us if our pastor's soul were going dry behind a growing church?
Where am I living like a cut branch, producing activity and calling it fruit?
Have we admired our pastor's refusal to stop, and in doing so quietly asked him to be a candle?
sessions.teaching:
Jesus once asked a question every ambitious pastor should keep where he reads it every day: "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?" (Mark 8:36). He wasn't speaking to stockbrokers. He was speaking to disciples who wanted to be great, and it lands hardest on people whose whole world is the work of God. A pastor can lose his soul building a kingdom and call the loss sacrifice. I'm not immune to that.

There's a way of leading a church that slowly hollows out the man leading it, and from the outside it looks like success. Attendance climbs. Staff grows. He's busy, sought after, effective. And inside, the well that fed it all is running dry, and he's preaching from memory of a God he used to know instead of from life with the God he has. A board needs to feel how invisible this is, because the numbers they watch are exactly the ones that hide it.

There's a real and good objection, and it should be heard first. Ministry is meant to cost. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. Paul said he was "being poured out as a drink offering" and rejoiced in it (Philippians 2:17). A pastor forever guarding his peace will never go to the hospital at two in the morning or bear what a flock sometimes does to the one who loves them. Sacrifice isn't the disease. It's the calling, and I won't back away from it.

But the objection mistakes what's being protected. The argument isn't that a pastor should spend himself less. It's that he has to be filled from a source the spending can't empty, or the spending becomes self-destruction instead of sacrifice. A candle gives light by consuming itself, and when it's gone, it's gone. A pastor isn't called to be a candle. He's called to be a branch, drawing life from the vine and bearing fruit because he's being fed. Cut the branch off and tell it to bear fruit by willpower, and you get a dead stick that calls its barrenness devotion.

"Abide in me, and I in you," Jesus says. "As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me" (John 15:4). Then comes the line we skip: "apart from me you can do nothing" (John 15:5). Not less. Not slightly weaker ministry. Nothing. The work of a cut branch amounts to nothing, however impressive it looks while it withers. The most frightening possibility in ministry is a man building something large and fruitless because he cut himself off from the vine to have more time to produce fruit.

The pressure has a recent history. From the 1970s on, the American church took on the language of corporate management. The pastor became the visionary and chief executive of a religious enterprise, and seminaries followed. Eugene Peterson called much of this a betrayal and compared such pastors to shopkeepers minding a religious store; a man can run a very good store and lose his soul behind the counter. The rabbi and family therapist Edwin Friedman argued that the most important thing in a leader isn't technique but what he called a non-anxious presence: the ability to stay connected to people without being swept up and driven by their anxiety. A pastor who hasn't tended his inner life picks up every fear in the congregation and vibrates with the room. He can't lead, because he has no ground to lead from.

Then there's the cross. First it exposes the lie under the overwork. If you can't rest, you don't really believe the work is God's, because if you believed God builds the house, you could sleep while he builds. "Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain," the psalm says, and then, "he gives to his beloved sleep" (Psalm 127:1-2). A pastor's sleeplessness preaches a sermon every night about who he thinks is in charge. But the cross also sets him free. "It is finished," Jesus said (John 19:30), and he meant it. Our frantic additions to a finished work aren't piety. The gospel frees a man to work hard because his identity doesn't ride on the work. He can pour himself out at a hospital bed at two in the morning and then go home and sleep without guilt, because his sleep is trust that the vine keeps feeding the branch while it rests.

scriptureStudy.note: "For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?" Spoken to disciples who wanted greatness. A man can win everything visible and lose the one thing meant to lead it.

"Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you." Fruit comes from being joined to the vine, never from effort cut off from the source.
"Apart from me you can do nothing." Not less. Nothing. For a busy pastor this may be the most frightening sentence in the chapter.

The branch that doesn't abide "is thrown away like a branch and withers." The picture is almost physical. A branch off the vine simply dries out, and no amount of willpower makes a cut branch bear fruit.
"Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain." A pastor's inability to rest says something about who he believes is really building the church.

"It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep." Sleep itself is a gift and an act of trust that God, not the anxious builder, holds the house through the night.
"It is finished." The decisive work was done by another. Our frantic additions to it aren't piety, and the cross is what finally lets the branch work hard and then rest.

sessions.goingDeeper:
A group that wants to go further can take the candle and the branch past metaphor. The cut branch producing a busy nothing isn't a warning against laziness. It's a warning against a particular kind of hard work: the activity of a man who has cut himself off from his source to get more hours of output. That's why the numbers a board trusts can hide the wound. Numbers measure the visible branch, not whether it's being fed.

Set Peterson beside Friedman. Peterson looks at what a pastor does, warning that the business of running a religious organization crowds out the patient care of souls. Friedman looks at who a pastor is: either a self grounded enough to lead, or a man so caught up in the congregation's moods that he simply amplifies its anxiety. Both point to the same hidden thing, the inner life, which is where leadership grows and the first thing a busy season strips away.

For a board the uncomfortable question is whether your own demands have been shaping your pastor into someone who just absorbs the room's anxiety. Every anxious expectation, every assumption that he's always available, every measure that rewards visible output presses him toward what Jesus calls nothing. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in Life Together (1938), bound solitude and community together and warned, in substance, that the person who can't be alone should beware of community (paraphrased). A man who can't be alone with God brings only an anxious, performing self into the church. A board that wants fruit has to learn to guard a root it will never see.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose your church has grown for three straight years. Your pastor launched a second service, added staff, and the board is proud, because every number on the report is up. At the annual review someone suggests a third service and a new outreach effort, since the pastor clearly can do more. A quieter elder hesitates. He's noticed the preaching has gone a little mechanical: polished but no longer warm, like a man working from the memory of a fire rather than standing near one. He can't prove it, and every number argues against him.

The board is watching the branch and can't see the root. A growing church can be led by a man whose soul is going dry, and the success itself can hide it. The real question isn't whether to add a third service. It's whether anyone in the room is close enough to know if the pastor is being fed or only burning, and whether the next request feeds the branch or strips it.

Resist the urge to load more onto a capable man. Ask instead what you could take off his plate, and whether your admiration for his output has been quietly asking him to be a candle.

memoryVerse.text: I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.

devotional.title: Gain the World, Lose the Soul
devotional.body:
Jesus asked, "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?" and he asked disciples who wanted to be great. The warning isn't only for the obviously worldly. It's for the ambitious servant whose whole world is the work of God, because he can lose his soul building a kingdom and call it sacrifice.

From the outside it looks like success. The projects multiply, the calendar fills, and the well runs dry without anyone noticing, least of all the man himself. Ask the question of your own life today. What world have you been gaining, and at what cost? Not the obvious sins, but the slow loss that wears the face of dedication. Jesus doesn't ask to shame the ambitious. He asks to save them before the trade is complete.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I can lose my soul in the very work I do for you and call it devotion. Show me where I've been gaining a world and losing myself. Stop me before the trade is complete.

devotional.title: Candle or Branch
devotional.body:
There are two ways to give light, and only one keeps you alive. A candle burns itself up. A branch bears fruit because it's fed. Jesus didn't call his people to be candles. "Abide in me, and I in you," he said. The fruit comes from the abiding, not the burning.

A church can love a candle down to the stub and call it dedication, and the man burning down can mistake his own disappearance for faithfulness. Ask today which one you've been trying to be, and which you've quietly asked others to be. Sometimes the cure for exhaustion is to do less. The deeper cure is to stop being a candle at all: to receive before you give, so what comes out of you is fruit and not the last of your own wax.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I've tried to be a candle and called my burning devotion. But you made me a branch, meant to bear fruit because I'm fed. Join me to the vine. Teach me to receive before I give.

devotional.title: Apart From Me, Nothing
devotional.body:
Read the line we skip: "Apart from me you can do nothing." Not less. Nothing. The work of a branch cut off from the vine adds up to nothing, however impressive it looks while it withers. A busy, fruitful-looking life could be a large, visible nothing if the connection at the root has been cut.

We measure ourselves by output. Jesus measures by connection, by whether the fruit grows from him or from our own dry effort. Ask today how much of what you're building is fed by life with Christ, and how much is the frantic work of a branch running on stored-up sap. The question isn't meant to condemn you but to call you back. The most diligent thing you can do isn't to work harder but to abide.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you said apart from you I can do nothing, and I've built as if I could do everything. Show me where I've cut myself off to produce more. Call me back to the vine.

devotional.title: Quietness and Trust
devotional.body:
Edwin Friedman, studying leaders, argued that the most important thing a leader brings is a calm presence: staying connected to people without being driven by their fear. A leader without that inner ground absorbs every anxiety in the room and can't lead, because he has nowhere to lead from.

Isaiah says it in older words: "In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength." And then the sad line: "But you were unwilling." The strength is in the quiet and the trust, and we keep refusing it because it looks like doing nothing. Notice today where you've been picking up everyone's anxiety and calling it care. The cure isn't to care less but to be more grounded, with an inner quiet the room's fear can't take over. Ask God for it.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I've vibrated with every fear around me and called it care. Give me the quietness and trust that are my strength. Let me stay close to anxious people without being ruled by their fear.

devotional.title: He Gives His Beloved Sleep
devotional.body:
"Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain." A pastor's sleeplessness can be a sermon he preaches to himself every night: that he, not God, is building the house. Then the psalm's tenderest line: "he gives to his beloved sleep." Sleep is named as a gift, the body lying down in trust that God holds the house through the night.

This is the gospel pressing into the most practical question there is: can you rest? "It is finished," Jesus said from the cross. Our frantic additions to a finished work are quiet unbelief. If God builds the house, you can work hard and then sleep, pour yourself out and then rest. Lie down tonight as an act of faith, and let your sleep say that Christ, not you, holds what you love.
devotional.prayer: Lord, my refusal to rest has been a sermon that I'm the one building the house. Forgive the unbelief dressed as diligence. You give your beloved sleep. Let me receive it. Amen.

sessions.title: The Interior Life
sessions.aim: To recognize that a pastor can handle the things of God all week and still starve, because handling isn't eating, and to protect the hidden life the whole ministry depends on.
sessions.summary:
There's a hunger that only strikes people who work with food all day: the cook surrounded by meals he never sits down to eat, the pastor surrounded by Scripture he only ever prepares for someone else. A pastor can stand in his study with an open Bible and realize he hasn't read a word of it for his own soul in weeks. He's read it for the sermon and the funeral, not as bread.

The inner life is the part of a pastor nobody sees and everything depends on, and because nobody sees it, it goes first. Some say this focus on inner life is a modern indulgence the apostles wouldn't recognize, and a spirituality always examining itself can turn sour. But Paul wrote that "our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16). And Jesus, with a whole town looking for him, rose "very early in the morning, while it was still dark" and went to a desolate place to pray (Mark 1:35).

He drew his public ministry from hidden time with his Father. We try to run a public ministry on an empty interior and wonder why it sounds hollow. The hidden life isn't preparation for the real work. It is the real work, and the public ministry is what overflows from it.

keyScripture.why: "And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed" (Mark 1:35). While the whole town looked for him, Jesus drew his public ministry from hidden time with the Father.

discussion.q: How can a pastor be soaked in Scripture all week and still be starving?
discussion.behind: Handling isn't eating. A pastor reads the text for the sermon and the funeral and never for his own bread. Being near holy things isn't the same as being fed by them; a man can be fluent in God and personally famished. Let the picture land before anyone suggests a solution.

discussion.q: A pastor's inner life pays no bills and fills no pews, so it gets fed last, and in a busy season not at all. What does it mean that the most important part of your pastor is the part your church never evaluates?
discussion.behind: Boards evaluate the public man because he's the one they can see. The hidden man is the soil the public man grows from, and because it's invisible it's the first thing sacrificed. Help the room see how its whole way of paying attention pushes the pastor to neglect what he can least afford to lose.

discussion.q: Read Mark 1:32-38. Jesus rose before dawn and went off to pray while everyone was looking for him. If the most needed man in Israel guarded his hidden life that fiercely, what does that ask of a board?
discussion.behind: "Everyone is looking for you" is the pressure every pastor knows, and Jesus chose the desolate place over the crowd. Is the board the crowd at the door, filling every hour? Move people toward protecting his time alone with God as a real duty.

discussion.q: As long as a pastor is preparing, he's the one handling the text, not the one it's speaking to. Where might busyness be a way of hiding from what God would say to us, not just a full calendar?
discussion.behind: This is the quieter, harder question. Time alone with God is where he tells us the truth about ourselves, and many of us would rather stay busy than be that exposed. A board can't fix that, but it can stop rewarding the busyness that helps a man hide. Invite people to see that this is true of board members too.

discussion.q: Many believers pray for years the way a tenant talks to a landlord before they learn to pray like a child talking to a glad father. What would help your pastor be a son here and not just a professional of holy things?
discussion.behind: See the pastor not as someone who dispenses God but as a child who needs to be fed by God, and ask what the church does that treats him otherwise. Go first with your own version of praying like a tenant. The point is communion, not performance.

objections.objection: This focus on the pastor's inner world is a modern indulgence. Paul didn't check his soul like a man taking his temperature every hour. He obeyed God and ran hard.
objections.response: There's truth in that. A spirituality always examining itself can turn into self-absorption, and the cure for an anxious pastor isn't always more introspection. But the objection misreads its own apostle. Paul wrote that "though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16). His running was fueled by a renewal in the hidden man. And the Lord himself, in a ministry more urgent than ours, rose before dawn to pray. If he needed it, the idea that we've outgrown it isn't maturity. It's presumption.

objections.objection: Our pastor's week is already full of urgent need. There's no time for hours of hidden prayer that produce nothing the church can see.
objections.response: Busy people ask this sincerely. But notice the assumption inside it: that the inner life is one more task to fit into a full schedule. It isn't an item on the list. It's the soil the whole list grows in, and a farmer doesn't ask when he'll find time to have soil. The man who skips it to plant more hours isn't more diligent. He's farming dust. A board's job isn't to add the inner life to the pastor's load but to clear ground so it has room to exist.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When did you last read a passage of Scripture for no reason but your own hunger, with no one to teach and nothing to prepare?
sessions.practice: This week, as a board, name one regular demand you place on the pastor's mornings and consider giving those mornings back to him, guarded and unscheduled, as time to be alone with God. Then leave it alone. Don't ask him to report on it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, our pastor handles holy things all week and can starve in the middle of them, and we've helped fill every hour so there's no quiet place left for him to pray. Forgive us. Teach us to guard his hidden life the way your Son guarded his, rising before dawn while the town still called his name. Feed the man in our pastor that no one sees and everything depends on. Let him come to you empty and be filled, as a son comes to a father who's glad he walked in. Amen.
reflection: Does our church treat the pastor's time alone with God as a duty to protect or as the first thing to interrupt?
Where am I using busyness, even good busyness, to keep from being known by God in the quiet?
Do I treat prayer and Scripture as bread for my own soul, or only as tools for a task?
sessions.teaching:
There's a particular hunger that only strikes people who work with food all day: the cook surrounded by meals he never sits down to eat, the pastor surrounded by Scripture he only ever prepares for someone else. A pastor can stand in his study on a Tuesday morning with an open Bible and realize, with a cold clarity, that he hasn't read a word of it for his own soul in weeks. He's read it for the sermon. He's read it for the funeral. He hasn't read it as bread.

The inner life is the part of a pastor nobody sees and everything depends on: the man as he is when the building is empty and nobody's watching him pray. And because nobody sees it, it's the first thing to go. A church pays for the public man and evaluates the public man. The inner man pays no bills and fills no pews, so he gets fed last, which in a busy season means not at all. A board should feel the trap in that. Its whole way of paying attention pushes the pastor to neglect the one thing he can least afford to lose.

There's a serious objection. Some would say this focus on the inner world is a modern indulgence, spiritual navel-gazing the apostles wouldn't have recognized. Paul didn't check his soul like a man taking his temperature every hour. He planted churches, took beatings, and ran hard. And a spirituality always examining itself really can turn into self-absorption. But the objection misreads its own apostle. Paul wrote, "Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16). He had an inner life and tended it, and his running was fueled by that daily renewal.

And the objection forgets the Lord himself. In Mark 1 Jesus has healed all evening while "the whole city was gathered together at the door" (Mark 1:33). The next morning, "rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed" (Mark 1:35). The disciples come hunting for him and say, almost scandalized, "Everyone is looking for you" (Mark 1:37). That's the pressure every pastor knows: everyone is looking for you, and the needs are stacking up at the door. And the Son of God had chosen the quiet place over the waiting crowd, because he couldn't be what the crowd needed without first being alone with his Father. He drew his public ministry from hidden communion. We try to run a public ministry on an empty interior and then wonder why our preaching sounds hollow.

Ruth Haley Barton describes leaders who come to treat prayer and Scripture as tools for ministry instead of ways to be with God, until they're leading on empty. Dallas Willard spent his life arguing that what's missing is a real apprenticeship to Jesus in the practices of the inner life; we've taught people to explain the bread without teaching them to eat it. The hidden life isn't preparation for the real work. It is the real work, and the public ministry is its overflow.

There's a quieter reason we avoid it, and naming it is half the cure. The quiet room is where God deals with us about ourselves, and many of us would rather stay busy than be that exposed. As long as a man is preparing a sermon he's safe. He's the one with the answers, handling the text instead of being its subject. The moment he sits in the dark with nothing to prepare, the text turns and starts reading him, and what it finds isn't always flattering. Busyness can be a way of running from that, and a pastor can hide from his own soul behind the very Scriptures he preaches.

To handle holy things professionally without being with the Holy One personally is to be a tour guide pointing at a country he's never entered. But the cross opened that country. When Jesus died, "the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Mark 15:38), and the holiest place was opened to people with dirty hands and divided hearts. You don't have to assemble a worthy inner life before you come in. You come in empty, and the coming in is how you're filled.

scriptureStudy.note: All evening "the whole city was gathered together at the door," and Jesus healed many. The public demand is huge and legitimate, which is what makes the next verse so striking.

"Rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark." He guards the hidden time before the demands wake. He doesn't fit prayer into the gaps of the day. He gives it the day's first and most protected hour.
"He departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed." He chooses the quiet place on purpose, away from the crowd that needs him.

"Simon and those who were with him searched for him, and they found him and said to him, 'Everyone is looking for you.'" Here's the pressure every pastor knows: the crowd at the door, and the mild scandal of withdrawing from it to pray.
"Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also." He answers out of his time with the Father, not out of the crowd's demand. The hidden hour ordered the public day.

"Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day." Paul names a hidden self being fed daily, the renewal that fueled his running. That answers the charge that the inner life is a modern indulgence.

sessions.goingDeeper:
A group that wants to go further can ask why the inner life is the first thing sacrificed. The reason isn't laziness but design. A church pays for, evaluates, and rewards the visible man, and the hidden man produces nothing anyone can measure, so every incentive a board creates pushes the pastor to starve the part of himself everything else grows from. Barton's phrase "leading on empty" names where that ends.

Willard sharpened the diagnosis. Much evangelical preaching, he argued in The Divine Conspiracy (1998), shrank the gospel to a transaction about the afterlife and lost the present reality of life with God. And there's a harder layer underneath: avoiding the inner life is often avoiding being known by God. A board can't fix that. But it can stop rewarding the busyness that helps a man hide, and it can refuse to treat his time alone with God as the first thing to interrupt.

Peterson, in Working the Angles (1987), called prayer, Scripture, and spiritual direction the "angles" of pastoral work: unseen lines that determine whether the visible shape of a ministry is true or bent. Skip them and the structure looks fine for a while, then slowly goes crooked, and everyone sees the crookedness while no one can name the cause, because the cause is hidden. That's what a board is asked to guard: a man's hidden life with God, which it will never see and on which everything it can see depends.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose your pastor's mornings have quietly filled. A standing staff meeting at eight, hospital visits, a discipleship breakfast, a building committee call. All good things, added one at a time over two years with the board's blessing. He used to guard the early hours for study and prayer. Nobody decided to take them. They just got filled, one reasonable demand at a time. At a planning meeting someone proposes a new men's prayer breakfast, also on a weekday morning, and the pastor agrees right away, because he agrees to everything.

The board has become the crowd at the door, filling every hour and never meaning harm. If the most needed man in Israel withdrew from the waiting crowd to pray, a board that loves its pastor has to ask whether it has left him a single unscheduled morning to be alone with God.

The faithful move goes against instinct. Instead of adding the breakfast, give a morning back. Guard it, leave it unscheduled, and then leave it alone. Don't ask him to report on what he does with it. You can't add the hidden life to his load. You can only stop crowding it out.

memoryVerse.text: And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed.

devotional.title: The Cook Who Never Eats
devotional.body:
There's a hunger that only strikes people who work with food all day: the cook who never sits down to eat, the pastor who only prepares Scripture for someone else. A person can be soaked in the Bible all week and starve, because handling isn't eating.

Jeremiah says, "Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart." He ate them. He didn't only study them or deliver them. That danger isn't only for pastors. Anyone who teaches or leads can come to treat Scripture as material. Ask today when you last read a passage for nothing but your own hunger. Then open the Bible not to harvest something from it but to be fed by it.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I can handle your word all day and never eat it. Teach me to take your words in as food and not as material. Let them become the joy and delight of my heart.

devotional.title: While It Was Still Dark
devotional.body:
Jesus had healed all evening with the whole town at the door. The next morning, "while it was still dark," he went to a desolate place to pray. The most needed man in Israel withdrew from the need to be with his Father, and he did it before the demands woke.

We do the opposite. We give the early hours to the demands and try to find God in whatever's left, and there's never anything left. If the Son of God needed the quiet place, we haven't outgrown it. Look today at where your time with God sits in your day. Is it first and guarded, or does it get the scraps? Consider giving God the early, protected hour, and drawing the day out of it.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you rose in the dark to be with your Father, and I give you only what's left. Forgive the order of my days. Teach me to guard the first hour.

devotional.title: Everyone Is Looking for You
devotional.body:
When the disciples found Jesus praying, they were almost scandalized: "Everyone is looking for you." It's the pressure every servant of others knows, the sense that stepping away means failing the people at the door. But Jesus had stepped away so he'd know what to do next, and he answered them out of his prayer, not out of their panic.
