The voice that says everyone is looking for you is loud, and it isn't wrong that the needs are real. But it isn't the voice you obey first. Today, when the pressure rises to be endlessly available, remember that the most useful version of you is drawn from time alone with God. Withdrawing to pray isn't abandoning people. It's the only way to have something real to give them when you come back.
devotional.prayer: Lord, the voice saying everyone needs me is loud, and I obey it before I obey you. Teach me to withdraw without guilt, and to come back with something real.

devotional.title: When the Text Reads You
devotional.body:
There's a quieter reason we avoid time alone with God. It's where he deals with us about ourselves, and many of us would rather stay busy than be that exposed. As long as you're preparing, you're safe, the one handling the text. Open it in the dark for your own soul and it starts reading you.

"The word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword," and "no creature is hidden from his sight." Busyness can be a way of hiding from being known that completely. Ask today whether your good, holy busyness keeps you on the safe side of Scripture. Come to it with nothing to prepare, and let it tell you the truth about yourself. The one who searches you that deeply was pierced for you and loves you on the other side of it.
devotional.prayer: Lord, your word is living and active, and I've stayed on the safe side of it. Forgive the busyness I hide behind. Let your word read me today, and meet me with mercy.

devotional.title: Come In Empty
devotional.body:
When Jesus died, the temple curtain tore from top to bottom. Hebrews says we now "have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us," so "let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith."

Here's the mercy that undoes every excuse. Your access to God isn't earned by the quality of your inner life. Christ bought it, and he offers it to you empty. You don't have to assemble a worthy inner life before you come in. You come in empty, and that's how you're filled. Many believers pray for years like a tenant talking to a landlord before they learn to pray like a child to a glad father. Stop waiting until you feel ready. Come in.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, you tore the curtain and opened the way, and I keep waiting to be worthy. Let me draw near empty, as a child to a glad father, and fill me as I come. Amen.

sessions.title: Why Your Church Should Require Rest
sessions.aim: To move a board from permitting rest to requiring it in writing, because the pastor who needs it most will refuse it, and to ground that requirement in the Sabbath God built into creation.
sessions.summary:
Many churches will let a pastor work himself into the ground and call it dedication. "We need you. We couldn't do it without you." The congregation means it as love, and it can crush him.

Churches shouldn't merely permit sabbaticals. They should require them, in writing, because a driven pastor who is free to decline rest will decline it, and the man who most needs it is the one most likely to refuse to prove he doesn't. A small church will say it can't afford the cover, and some will add that the New Testament knows nothing of pastoral sabbaticals. Those are fair objections. But the expensive thing isn't the sabbatical. It's the burned-out pastor you keep in the pulpit because resting him felt unaffordable.

Scripture builds rest into creation itself: God "rested on the seventh day from all his work" and "blessed the seventh day and made it holy" (Genesis 2:2-3), not because he was tired but to set a rhythm his creatures need. A pastor who won't rest is quietly claiming to be stronger than the God who stopped. And a pastor who rests preaches something true by his absence: Christ holds this church, not me.

keyScripture.why: "So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation" (Genesis 2:3). God didn't rest from need. He set a rhythm into creation that his creatures need, so a pastor who refuses rest is acting as if he were stronger than his Creator.

discussion.q: "We couldn't do it without you." How can a compliment a church means with love do real harm?
discussion.behind: The board's real affection can be the thing that crushes him, by leaning on the man they can't afford to lose. The compliment makes being indispensable feel like a virtue, which makes rest feel like betrayal. Help people see the danger hidden in their gratitude.

discussion.q: Why might the pastor who most needs rest refuse it when it's only offered?
discussion.behind: Asking for rest feels like admitting weakness to the people who evaluate him, so a driven man will wear himself out to avoid it. For a board, the conclusion is practical: take the rest out of his discretion and require it, the way a wise father takes the car keys from a son too proud to admit he's too tired to drive. Press toward the word "required," in writing.

discussion.q: Read Genesis 2:1-3 and Exodus 20:8-11. God rested on the seventh day, not because he was tired, but to set a rhythm into creation. What does it say about a pastor who won't rest?
discussion.behind: This is the theological spine. The Sabbath was built into creation before there was any church to run, so refusing it isn't extra holiness. Help the board see that requiring the pastor's rest isn't a worldly perk but obedience to the order God made.

discussion.q: Edwin Friedman observed that anxious organizations tend to lean hardest on their most responsible leader. Where might this church be leaning on your pastor without meaning to?
discussion.behind: A church can love its pastor into the ground just by leaning and never telling him to stop. Ask people to name the specific places: the calls, the expectations, the assumption that he's always available. Then own them.

discussion.q: Many pastors work through every Sabbath and call it love for the church, when underneath it's a refusal to trust that God can run the church for a day without them. Where do you see that refusal, in your pastor or in yourselves?
discussion.behind: Go first. Being indispensable is a sweeter idol than money and harder to give up, because people keep praising it. The freedom on offer is that if Christ holds the church, the pastor and the board can finally put it down and sleep.

objections.objection: We're a small church with one pastor and no staff to cover. We can't afford a three-month sabbatical without risking a collapse in giving and attendance.
objections.response: That fear is real, and it comes from people who love their church. Yes, rest costs something. So does a funeral. So does a pastoral search. So does the slow decline of a church led for a decade by a man running on fumes. The expensive thing isn't the sabbatical. It's the burned-out pastor you keep because resting him felt unaffordable. And it can start modestly. Even a small church can build toward a guarded month away every few years, with elders covering the pulpit and pastoral care. The size of the church doesn't change the command to rest. It only changes how creative you have to be to keep it.

objections.objection: The New Testament knows nothing of pastoral sabbaticals. Paul never took one. This is an academic perk dressed up in spiritual language.
objections.response: Take that seriously, and then look further back than the New Testament. Scripture builds rest into creation itself: God rested on the seventh day and made it holy. The Sabbath is the fourth commandment, in the same list as the commands against idolatry and murder. The law even gave the land a sabbatical: "in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land" (Leviticus 25:4). The academic sabbatical takes its very name from that practice. The church isn't importing a worldly perk. It's recovering something it forgot it had.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your pastor stepped fully away for a month, would you trust that Christ still holds this church? Or have you quietly come to believe the pastor does?
sessions.practice: This week, begin drafting language for your bylaws or governing documents that requires the pastor to rest: a guarded sabbatical on a set rhythm, out of his discretion. Make rest a rule in your church before exhaustion makes your pastor a casualty.
sessions.closingPrayer: God who rested on the seventh day, not because you were weak but to teach your creatures how to live, forgive us for asking our pastor to be stronger than you. Forgive the leaning we never meant as harm. Give us courage to write his rest into our rules, to take it out of his hands so his pride can't refuse it, and to trust that you hold this church whether or not he's in the room. Teach all of us to stop, because the work that saves the world is finished. Amen.
reflection: Have we treated our pastor's refusal to rest as a virtue? What would it cost us to call it what it is?
Where am I leaning on my pastor without meaning to, and what could I stop asking of him?
Do I believe Christ holds this church, or have I let myself believe the pastor does? How would the answer change the way I lead?
sessions.teaching:
Many churches will let a pastor work himself into the ground and call it dedication. The same church that would never ask a member to work ten years without real rest will ask exactly that of the man who shepherds it, and it will frame the asking as a compliment. "We need you. We couldn't do it without you." I suspect that sentence has buried more pastors than scandal has, and the congregations that said it stood at the graveside honestly confused about what went wrong.

So here's a practical argument with a theological backbone. Churches shouldn't merely permit sabbaticals. They should require them, in writing, the way an airline requires a pilot to rest before flying you across an ocean. A sabbatical that a driven pastor is free to decline will be declined, because the man who most needs rest is the one most likely to refuse it to prove he doesn't. Rest has to be required and taken out of his hands, or the men who need it most will wear themselves out avoiding it.

The objections deserve their full weight, because they're sincere and common. A small church says plainly it can't afford this. One pastor, no staff to cover, and a three-month absence could mean a drop in giving and attendance a small congregation might not recover from. There's a theological version too: the New Testament knows nothing of pastoral sabbaticals, Paul never took one, and this is a borrowed academic perk in church clothes. These aren't foolish objections, and they come from people who love their churches.

Answer the cost truthfully. Yes, it costs something. So does a funeral. So does a pastoral search. So does the slow decline of a congregation led for ten years by a man running on fumes who has quietly stopped meeting God. The expensive thing isn't the sabbatical. It's the burned-out pastor you keep in the pulpit because resting him felt unaffordable.

Then the theology. Scripture puts rest in the order of creation, before there was ever a church to run. "On the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done. So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy" (Genesis 2:2-3). He didn't rest because he was tired. He set a rhythm into the world that his creatures need to the bottom of their being. The Sabbath is the fourth commandment, in the same list as the commands against idolatry and murder, and the reason given is creation itself: "For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day" (Exodus 20:11). A pastor who won't rest isn't more spiritual than his Creator. He's quietly claiming to be stronger than the God who stopped.

Zack Eswine names the lie underneath the refusal: the belief that a pastor must be a kind of god for his people, everywhere for everyone, without limits. Health, he argues, begins with admitting we're creatures and not the Creator. Friedman observed that anxious organizations push their most responsible leaders into doing more and more, leaning on them until they break. A church can love its pastor straight into the ground without meaning any harm, just by leaning and leaning and never telling him to stop. Requiring rest is how a wise body stops leaning on the man it can't afford to lose.

And here's what turns it around. The pastor who never rests isn't serving the church best. Week after week he's teaching it that a human being holds the church together, which is about the most dangerous thing a congregation can learn. A pastor who rests preaches something truer by his absence, because his absence says out loud what his frantic presence denied: Christ holds this church. Not me.

The cross does two things here. First it names the idol: the pastor's own indispensability, which sounds more spiritual than money or sex and is harder to give up, because people keep praising it. The church has one head, and it isn't the pastor. Then it sets him free. If Christ holds the church, the pastor and the board can finally put it down and sleep. "There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God" (Hebrews 4:9). The gospel isn't a summons to work harder for God. In the end it's an invitation to stop, because the work that saves the world is finished. So write the sabbatical into the bylaws.

scriptureStudy.note: "On the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day." The God who doesn't tire chose to stop. Rest is part of the creation account, before sin and before the church.
"So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy." Rest isn't merely allowed. It's blessed and set apart, built into creation as a rhythm creatures need.

"Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work." The command sits among the commands against idolatry and murder. Rest is a matter of obedience, not preference.
"For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth ... and rested on the seventh day." The reason given is creation itself, so the rhythm isn't a cultural habit but part of how the world is made.
"In the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land." Even the ground is told to lie fallow. The sabbatical idea is biblical before it's academic.

"There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God's rest has also rested from his works as God did from his." In the end rest is the gospel: a stopping that confesses the saving work belongs to another.

"It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest ... for he gives to his beloved sleep." The frantic schedule is called vain, and sleep is a gift that confesses God, not the worker, holds the house.

sessions.goingDeeper:
A group that wants to go further can look at what it means to be a creature. The Sabbath isn't first a management practice. It's a confession that we're creatures and not the Creator. In The Imperfect Pastor (2015), Zack Eswine traces much pastoral overwork to the belief that a pastor must be a kind of god for his people, everywhere and without limits. Refusing rest is, underneath, refusing to be a creature.

Set that beside Friedman's observation that anxious organizations lean hardest on their most responsible leader, and a board can see why rest has to be taken out of the pastor's hands. The man who needs it most can't ask for it, because asking feels like confessing weakness to the people who evaluate him.

The church is also recovering its own forgotten practice, not importing a worldly one. The academic sabbatical takes its name from the Sabbath and the sabbatical year in Leviticus, when the land lay fallow so the soil wouldn't be exhausted. The world borrowed the idea from Scripture and kept it, and now the church sometimes eyes its own inheritance with suspicion. And the sharpest point is about being indispensable. The belief that a church can't survive its pastor's rest isn't humility. It's a claim to a headship that belongs to Christ alone. A board that requires rest isn't handing out a benefit. It's taking down an idol, for the pastor's sake and its own, and teaching the whole congregation, through the pastor's guarded absence, that Christ holds the church.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose your pastor has served faithfully for twelve years and never taken more than a week away. The board loves him and tells him so, often: "You're the heart of this church. We couldn't do it without you." He lights up a little when they say it, and he has turned down every gentle suggestion of a longer break, insisting he's fine and the church needs him. This year an elder proposes writing a required sabbatical into the bylaws: a guarded month away every few years, with the elders covering the pulpit and pastoral care. Another elder pushes back. It might look like they're pushing the pastor out, he says, and the pastor keeps saying he doesn't want it.

The pastor's refusal is exactly why the rest has to be required and not just offered. The man who needs it most will decline it to prove he doesn't. And the loving compliment, "we couldn't do it without you," is part of the weight on him.

Don't wait for him to ask. He never will. Take the rest out of his hands and write it down, the way a wise father takes the keys. Make rest a rule in your church before exhaustion makes your pastor a casualty, and trust that Christ holds the church whether or not the pastor is in the room.

memoryVerse.text: So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation.

devotional.title: We Couldn't Do It Without You
devotional.body:
One of the heaviest sentences a pastor hears is a compliment: "We couldn't do it without you." The congregation means it with love, and that's what makes it heavy. It makes being indispensable feel like a virtue and rest feel like betrayal.

But God, who really could do everything alone and never tires, chose to stop on the seventh day. He rested, blessed the rest, and made it holy. If the God who holds the universe together rested, the person who refuses to rest isn't more faithful than his Creator. Look today at the compliments you give and receive. Have you leaned on someone by telling them how indispensable they are? Where has being needed become a trap for you? You're a creature. You're allowed to stop. The world is held by someone else.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I've made being needed my worth and leaned on others until they nearly broke. You held the universe and still you rested. Teach me I'm a creature, allowed to stop.

devotional.title: Stronger Than the God Who Stopped
devotional.body:
The Sabbath isn't tucked in the margins of Scripture. It's the fourth commandment, alongside the commands against idols and murder, and the reason given is creation: "in six days the LORD made heaven and earth ... and rested on the seventh day."

We break this one more easily than the others and feel good about it. No one praises a man for adultery, but congregations applaud a man who never takes a day off, and a sin that gets applauded is the hardest to turn from. Ask today whether you've treated your own refusal to rest, or someone else's, as holiness. Let the fourth commandment bind you as surely as the others, and ask for the humility to stop and be the creature God made you.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I've called my refusal to rest devotion and broken your command in the most applauded way. Forgive me. Give me the humility to stop as you stopped.

devotional.title: The Idol Called Indispensable
devotional.body:
Of all the idols we serve, being indispensable may be the sweetest, because it sounds so much like virtue. Nobody rebukes you for it, and many praise you. A pastor who believes the church can't survive his rest has quietly made himself its head.

But Paul says of Christ, "he is before all things, and in him all things hold together. And he is the head of the body, the church." Christ holds the church together. Not the pastor, not the board, not the volunteer who can't say no. Find the place today where your identity rests on being the one who holds it all together, at church, at work, or at home. It's exhausting because it asks you to do a job that was never yours. He held it before you came and will hold it after.
devotional.prayer: Lord Christ, you hold all things together and you're the head of the church, not me. Take down my idol of being indispensable, and free me to rest.

devotional.title: Required, Not Permitted
devotional.body:
Jesus saw that his disciples "had no leisure even to eat," because so many were coming and going, and he said, "Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while." He didn't offer it to whoever felt like it. He saw they were depleted and called them away.

The people who most need rest are usually the last to take it when it's merely allowed. Asking feels like weakness, so the most driven and faithful decline it to prove they don't need it. That's why love sometimes has to make rest required. Is there someone whose rest you need to protect by taking it out of their hands? And are you the one who won't rest unless someone makes you? Let yourself be called away.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you saw your tired disciples and called them away. Give me love to protect the rest of those who won't claim it, and the humility to be called away myself.

devotional.title: The Work That Saves Is Finished
devotional.body:
"There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God's rest has also rested from his works as God did from his." The deepest reason you can stop isn't that your work is done. It's that the work that matters most was finished by someone else.

A pastor who rests and lets the church go on a season without him says out loud what his frantic presence denied: Christ holds this church. Not me. The same is true of whatever you're gripping too tightly. Today, enter that rest a little. Put down one thing you've been carrying as if everything depended on you. Take the day off you've been refusing. Sleep as an act of faith. The rest remains, and it's for you.
devotional.prayer: Lord, the work that saves the world is finished, and still I labor as if it depended on me. Let me enter the rest that remains, and confess by my rest that you hold it all. Amen.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here, and for caring enough about your pastor to sit in this. Before we start, three things. First, this study isn't here to scold the pastor for being tired or this board for not noticing. It asks us to look at a way of doing church we helped build, and none of us is outside it. Second, nobody has to perform certainty or strength. You can be unsure out loud, and you can change your mind. Third, this material touches burnout and, in two sessions, depression directly. Depression is an illness, not a failure of faith, and the faithful response to it is a doctor and a licensed counselor, the same as for any sickness of the body. If a pastor is ever in crisis, call or text 988. Seeking help is faith, not failure, and there is no shame in this room. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. I'll read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what this passage says. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into the way this church actually treats the man who shepherds it, because none of this matters if it stays an idea.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though it isn't resolved, and I'm not going to pretend it is. Take the weight of this out with you instead of leaving it at the door. Try the practice this week, and work through the reflection questions on your own. And if anything tonight made you worried about your pastor, or about yourself, don't carry it alone. A doctor and a counselor are faithful first steps, and in a crisis you call or text 988. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for being willing to tell the truth in this room.

leaderPrimer:
Before you plan a single meeting, notice who this study is about, because he may be sitting at your table. If your pastor is in the room with the board that employs him, understand what you're asking. You're asking a man whose income, housing, and public life depend on the people present to consider saying, in front of them, that he isn't okay. Every instinct he has trained for years tells him not to. He has performed strength through funerals and conflicts and his own dry seasons, and he'll watch the first two sessions the way a man tests ice before he puts his weight on it. That watching is the real content of your meetings, whatever the page says.

So your task as leader is almost entirely about safety, and safety is shown, not announced. It's shown when a board member goes first with his own exhaustion instead of inviting the pastor to bare his soul for the group. It's shown when something true comes out in session 2, on depression, and nobody rushes to fix it and nobody quietly recalculates the man's job security. One raised eyebrow, one follow-up question that sounds like an evaluation, and the ice closes for good. Then the study will finish politely, with everyone agreeing that rest is important.

Ban two sentences from your room. "We need you" can weigh a man down more than anyone means it to. And "he seems fine" is how churches often describe a man a few months before he resigns.

End where session 5 ends, with the church requiring rest instead of permitting it, because permission can be declined and a tired man will decline it every time. You aren't there to appreciate your pastor; appreciation is a coffee mug. You're there to become a room where a shepherd can be a sheep. If that happens even once in five weeks, it will outlast a lot of sermons.

faq.q: Is this study going to feel like the board putting our pastor on trial?
faq.a: It should never feel that way, and if it does, the leader has taken a wrong turn. The biggest danger in this study is letting it become a performance review, and the whole design works against that. It isn't a conversation about the pastor's job performance. It's an act of love toward the person who shepherds you. The material asks the board to look at a way of doing church it helped build, not at a tired employee to be assessed. The leader goes first, with his own exhaustion, before asking anything of the pastor. If at any point your pastor feels graded rather than loved, stop and say so, because no man will admit he's running on fumes to people he thinks are evaluating him.

faq.q: What if our pastor is in the room and doesn't want to open up?
faq.a: Then let him not open up, and mean it. The study works even if the pastor only listens. It names things he may have hidden for years, and hearing them in front of the people he performs wellness for can feel like exposure. Nothing here requires him to confess anything to the group. Make that clear by your tone and, if needed, out loud. Your job is to lower the cost of telling the truth, not to demand it, and the surest way is for board members to go first with their own. Don't mistake the board's appetite for openness for the pastor's readiness. He may need to watch the room be safe several times before he risks saying anything, and he may never say much at all. The study can still do its work in him.

faq.q: Does this study treat depression as a spiritual failure?
faq.a: No, and it works hard to strip that shame away. It names a pastor's depression plainly as an illness that can sit inside deep faith, the way despair sat in Elijah, Jeremiah, Job, and the Psalms. If despair were always faithlessness, the most faithful people in Scripture were the most faithless, which is absurd. Depression is an illness of body and mind, not a measure of anyone's faith, and the faithful response is the care of a doctor and a licensed counselor, as for any other illness. Seeking help is an act of faith, not a confession of failure, and there's no shame in it. Wherever the material meets depression or crisis, it points to medical and counseling care and keeps the crisis line in view. If a pastor is in crisis, call or text 988.

faq.q: When should we point someone toward a doctor or counselor rather than just praying with them?
faq.a: Whenever the struggle moves past ordinary discouragement toward what sounds like depression or another illness of body and mind, the answer is both, not either. Pray, and also help the person to a physician and a licensed counselor, as you would for chest pain or a broken bone. Prescribing only more prayer and a sterner devotional life for a depressed pastor can mean withholding the very bread God sent the angel to bake. You aren't a counselor, and you don't diagnose. Your job is to remove the shame, make professional help look like health, cover the cost where you can, and protect the person's time to get well. If there is any sign of danger to a person's life, you do not treat it as too private to touch. You stay with them and you call or text 988 without hesitation.

faq.q: What is the 988 number, and when do we use it?
faq.a: 988 is the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the United States, reachable by call or text, staffed to help anyone in a mental health crisis or thinking about harming themselves. You use it any time you're seriously worried about someone's safety, including your pastor's. You don't need to be certain, and you don't need to be a professional. If a person says anything that frightens you about their safety, or you sense real danger, act at once. Stay with them, and call or text 988. A board must never treat a pastor's life as too private to protect; acting quickly in a crisis is love, not intrusion. Keep the number where your leaders can find it, and say it out loud in the sessions that touch depression, so no one has to go looking for it in a moment when looking feels impossible.

faq.q: Why does the study keep pointing at the board instead of the struggling pastor?
faq.a: Because a study that pointed only at the pastor would turn into the performance review it's trying to avoid. A board can't call a man to openness from above him without the openness feeling like exposure. When board members look at the way of doing church they helped build, and admit their own tiredness and their own leaning on him, it becomes safe for the pastor to tell the truth too. You can't feed a man bread while standing over him in judgment. You feed him as a fellow creature who is also tired and also needs rest.

faq.q: Isn't talking about burnout just excusing pastors from the sacrifice ministry has always required?
faq.a: No. Sacrifice is the calling, and this study doesn't back away from it. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, and a pastor forever guarding his peace will never go to the hospital at two in the morning. But the question isn't whether a pastor spends himself. It's what he's being spent on and whether anything refills him. A man can be poured out for Christ and rest in him, or poured out for a congregation's approval and be consumed by a god that blesses nothing. The first is sacrifice. The second is a slow death we've learned to call dedication. The cure isn't less burning but becoming a branch fed by the vine instead of a candle burning itself up. Naming burnout isn't excusing weakness. It's telling the truth about which master a man is spending himself for.

faq.q: We're a small church with one pastor. How could we possibly require a sabbatical?
faq.a: That fear comes from people who love their church, and it deserves a real answer. Yes, rest costs something. So does a funeral, a pastoral search, or the slow decline of a church led for a decade by a man running on fumes. The expensive thing isn't the sabbatical. It's the burned-out pastor you keep because resting him felt unaffordable. The shape can be modest. Even a small church can build toward a guarded month away every few years, with elders covering the pulpit and pastoral care. The size of the church doesn't change the Sabbath God built into creation. It only changes how creative you have to be. Start smaller than three months if you must, but start, and write it down so it can't be quietly declined.

faq.q: Why require rest in writing instead of just offering it?
faq.a: Because the pastor who most needs rest is the one who'll refuse it when it's only offered. Asking for rest feels like admitting weakness to the people who evaluate him, so a driven, faithful man will wear himself out to avoid it. A sabbatical he's free to decline will be declined. So it has to be taken out of his discretion and made automatic, written into the bylaws, the way a wise father takes the car keys from a son too proud to admit he's too tired to drive. That isn't the board imposing a burden. It's lifting one. Jesus didn't wait for his worn-out disciples to ask. He saw their exhaustion and called them away to rest (Mark 6:31).

faq.q: How do we tell the difference between a pastor who's just tired and one who's in real danger?
faq.a: You don't have to make that call alone, and you shouldn't try. Ordinary tiredness lifts with rest: a real break, a meal, a good night's sleep, a load taken off. What should concern you is weariness that doesn't lift: the man who can't find a reason to care, who has gone quiet and flat, who hints that he can't see the point of getting up. Those are signs of something deeper than fatigue, and they call for a physician and a licensed counselor, not just a vacation. And if he says anything at all that frightens you about his safety, don't weigh it or wait. You stay with him, and you call or text 988. When in doubt, lean toward care. It's far better to walk a tired man toward help he didn't strictly need than to miss a man in danger.

faq.q: I'm not a counselor or a theologian. How can I lead this?
faq.a: You lead it the way it was built to be led, as a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every discussion question has a note behind it, every session has a case to talk through, and every session ends in prayer. But the real qualification isn't training. It's being willing to go first, to tell the truth about your own exhaustion, to keep the room safe and confidential, and to refuse to turn the study into an evaluation of your pastor. A board member who has named his own tiredness can lead this faithfully with no degree. A leader with three degrees who stands above the room assessing the pastor will do harm. Read this primer, settle your own heart, hold the guardrails about depression and the 988 line, and trust the material to carry the rest.

faq.q: Will this study make our pastor feel worse by dredging all this up?
faq.a: It can, if it's led carelessly, which is why the leader's posture matters so much. Run as a performance review or a group interrogation, it could feel like exposure and shame, and you need to guard against that with everything you have. But led as an act of love that includes the whole room and removes the shame from exhaustion and depression, it does the opposite. It tells your pastor that the people around him see what he carries, that they don't read his tiredness as failure, that getting help is faith, and that he doesn't have to perform fine anymore. Many pastors have never heard their leadership say those things. Done with confidentiality, with the leader going first and no demand that the pastor confess anything, the study is more likely to lift a burden than add one.

faq.q: What do we actually do after the study ends?
faq.a: Turn it into something concrete, gently, without making it one more program. The practices in the sessions point the way. Find out whether the church covers counseling for the pastor and his family, and whether he has a physician and a counselor he actually sees; if not, start making it yes. Look at what you ask of his mornings and consider giving guarded, unscheduled time back to him. Begin drafting language that requires rest, a guarded sabbatical on a set rhythm, written into your governing documents. And quietly, without alarm, make sure someone in the room is close enough to the pastor to know how he really is. The point isn't a thick action plan. It's a few lasting changes that take the weight off him and make help and rest a normal part of his life instead of emergency measures.

timeline.event: Charles Spurgeon publishes Lectures to My Students, including "The Minister's Fainting Fits," where the famous preacher writes without shame about his own depression: "Fits of depression come over the most of us."

Anton Boisen, a minister who had himself been hospitalized for mental illness, begins bringing theological students to train at Worcester State Hospital in Massachusetts, the beginning of what became clinical pastoral education.
Henri Nouwen publishes The Wounded Healer, describing the minister whose own wounds, offered rather than hidden, become a source of healing for others.
The psychologist Herbert Freudenberger publishes early work describing "burnout" among people in helping professions, giving a name to what many pastors had long suffered without words.
Christina Maslach and Susan Jackson publish the Maslach Burnout Inventory, measuring burnout as emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and a reduced sense of accomplishment.
Eugene Peterson publishes Working the Angles (1987) and The Contemplative Pastor (1989), arguing that a pastor's real work is the unhurried care of souls, not running a religious business.
Marva Dawn publishes Keeping the Sabbath Wholly, part of a wider recovery of the Sabbath as God's gift and command rather than legalism.

Edwin Friedman's A Failure of Nerve is published after his death in 1996. It argues that a leader's calm, differentiated presence matters more than technique, and that anxious systems lean on their most responsible leaders.
The Duke Endowment funds the Duke Clergy Health Initiative, a long-term study of the physical and mental health of United Methodist pastors in North Carolina.
Ruth Haley Barton publishes Strengthening the Soul of Your Leadership, describing leaders who treat prayer and Scripture as tools until they're leading on empty.
Lifeway Research releases a study on acute mental illness and Christian faith, finding that nearly a quarter of pastors have personally struggled with some kind of mental illness.
Zack Eswine publishes The Imperfect Pastor, naming the belief that a pastor must be a kind of god for his people and grounding health in admitting we're creatures, not the Creator.
Barna reports that 38 percent of Protestant pastors had seriously considered quitting full-time ministry in the previous year.

The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline launches in the United States as a three-digit number reachable by call or text, making crisis help simpler to summon than at any earlier point in this conversation.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set ground rules, say plainly that this study touches depression and that getting help is faith, and take session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, Why Pastors Are Leaving.
Week 3: Session 2, Depression in the Pulpit, with unhurried time on the clinical turn and the 988 note.
Week 4: Session 2 continued: the wounded healer, and concrete steps to cover counseling and remove shame.
Week 5: Session 3, Leading Without Losing the Soul.
Week 7: Session 5, Why Your Church Should Require Rest, with time to start drafting bylaw language.
Week 8: Bringing it together. Look back over the five practices and agree on one concrete commitment this board will make for the pastor's health.

Week 4: Session 5, Why Your Church Should Require Rest, with a short closing time to name one commitment the board will make.

furtherReading: Lectures to My Students, Charles Spurgeon, especially "The Minister's Fainting Fits," for a Victorian preacher describing his own depression without shame.
Life Together, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, on solitude and community, a short and searching read for a leadership team. Behind session 3.
The Divine Conspiracy, Dallas Willard, for readers who want to press session 4's claim that life with God is the missing apprenticeship, not an optional extra.
Zeal Without Burnout, Christopher Ash, a short, gentle book a board could hand to a tired pastor, on the difference between godly sacrifice and self-destruction.
Resilient Ministry, Bob Burns, Tasha Chapman, and Donald Guthrie, a research-based resource for boards on the practices that keep pastors healthy over the long haul.

glossary.definition: The slow collapse of a person worn down by sustained demand without enough rest or renewal. In a pastor it often hides behind faithfulness and looks like dedication until it doesn't. It's a condition to be cared for, never a character flaw to be shamed.

A medical illness affecting mood, body, and mind, not a measure of someone's faith. It calls for the care of a doctor and a licensed counselor, the same as any other illness of the body. If a pastor is in crisis, call or text 988.
The particular weariness of people who carry others' pain for a living, when empathy runs dry from constant draining. Pastors are exposed to it through years of absorbing grief, crisis, and conflict.

The rhythm of rest God built into creation when he rested on the seventh day and blessed it. For a pastor it isn't a reward for finishing the work but a command and a gift that says God, not the pastor, holds the church.

An extended, deliberate season of rest from the steady demand of ministry, named for the Sabbath and the sabbatical year when the land lay fallow. This study argues a church should require it in writing, because the pastor who needs it most will refuse it if it's merely allowed.
A simple, settled set of practices (prayer, rest, Scripture, friendship) a person commits to so their life with God isn't crowded out by urgent demands. It guards the inner life session 4 describes.

The hidden part of a person, as they are before God when no one is watching, with nothing to prepare or perform. In a pastor it's the soil the public ministry grows from, and because no one sees it, it's the first thing to be starved.

Edwin Friedman's term for a leader's ability to stay connected to people without being driven by their anxiety, leading from settled inner ground. A pastor without it picks up every fear in the congregation.
Friedman's phrase for the steadiness a differentiated leader brings into an anxious group: staying calm and connected without being swallowed by the room's fear.

The difference between the calling to be a pastor, a shepherd of souls, and the role of running a religious organization. Peterson warned that a man can be very good at the role without ever having been a pastor, and that confusing the two lies behind much burnout.

Nouwen's picture of the minister whose own wounds, offered rather than hidden, become a source of healing for others. A pastor who has been to the floor and found God still there can keep company with suffering people without flinching.
The old name for the heart of pastoral work: patiently caring for individual people before God, as distinct from managing programs and budgets. Recovering it is part of recovering pastoral health.

Jesus' picture in John 15 of a branch drawing life continually from the vine, a settled dwelling in him rather than an occasional visit. A pastor bears real fruit only as he's fed; apart from the vine he can do nothing.

The belief, sweeter and more spiritual-sounding than other idols, that a church can't survive without this particular pastor. This study names it as the idol behind the refusal to rest, put down only when a board and a pastor remember who the real Shepherd is.
